title: What If You Could See Everyone's IQ?
description: What if you could see everyone's IQ floating above their heads? Imagine having a genius-level IQ of 160 but still failing your exams, while the smartest-looking student in class gets straight A's with only 70 IQ. But when the two compete to prove who's actually smarter, things take an unexpected turn. Does having a higher IQ really make you smarter, or is there more to intelligence than just a number?

art_style: Flat 2D vector 'stick-figure with a black ball head' style (the same family as the viral 'What if you...' stickman channels): every character is a solid black circle head with simple white oval eyes and eyebrow strokes (no other face features; mouth drawn as a small white shape only when talking/shocked), thin black limbs, and a coloured clothing shape that identifies them (protagonist = mustard-yellow hoodie; Oliver = navy blazer + red tie + slicked hair stripes; Jake = curly black hair + red/orange top; mom = glasses; principal = white hair + brown coat). Backgrounds are detailed flat-vector rooms (classroom, hallway lockers, library, bedroom, kitchen, street, auditorium) with heavy depth-of-field blur behind close-ups. Recurring device: a rounded pill tag above a head, green for high IQ ('160 IQ', '112 IQ') and red for low ('70 IQ', '94 IQ'), with a small pointer triangle. Explanatory beats cut to a dark navy 'infographic' card with thin white line-art icons and outlined text chips. Time/place cards are small uppercase captions bottom-left or top-left ('THAT MORNING / MY ROOM · 7:15 A.M.', 'THREE HOURS LATER'). Flashbacks are desaturated/greyscale.

title_pattern.template: What If You Could See Everyone's <hidden personal number/attribute>?
title_pattern.notes: Second-person 'What If You Could See…' superpower premise where the power reveals a hidden number about other people (IQ here; same family as 'see everyone's lifespan / bank balance / crush'). Six words, no number in the title: the numbers live on the thumbnail. The title promises a world-building comedy, the video delivers a moral story (number vs. effort) - title sells the gimmick, story pays it off.
reusable_variants: What If You Could See Everyone's <Net Worth / Lifespan / Lie Count / Social Credit>?
What If Everyone Had Their <Number> Above Their Head?

thumbnail.composition: Two-shot classroom, two characters side by side at desks facing camera-left, each with a glowing number above the head pointing down at them. Left: protagonist slumped, chin on hand, pencil, failed paper with big red circled 'F' at bottom-left. Right: rival in school blazer, smug side-eye, holding up a test with a big red circled 'A+'. Background: blurred classmates, chalkboard, sunlit window (warm golden backlight).
thumbnail.text: '160 IQ' (glowing neon green, top-centre-left) and '70 IQ' (glowing neon red, top-right), each with a down-pointing triangle. No other words; the 'F' and 'A+' grades are the second text layer.
thumbnail.colours: Warm golden-hour classroom (orange/brown) vs. saturated mustard-yellow hoodie and navy blazer; neon green vs. neon red labels as the main contrast pair; red ink on white paper for grades.
thumbnail.subject_scale_contrast: Irony contrast rather than scale: high number + F vs. low number + A+. Both faces large (each head ~25% of frame width), readable emotions (sad vs. smug). The thumbnail is a premium 3D/clay render of the stickman characters (textured ball heads, real cloth), much higher fidelity than the flat 2D video - a deliberate upgrade to stand out in the feed.
thumbnail.why_it_works: It is a one-glance paradox: the viewer reads 160 next to F and 70 next to A+ and instantly asks 'how?'. Green=good/red=bad colour coding is pre-attentive, the grades double the irony, and the faces tell you who feels what. It shows exactly the cold-open scene, so the click is rewarded in the first 30 s.

hook.first_5s_verbatim: The smartest kid in my school had an IQ of 70 and he was currently laughing at my test.
hook.first_30s_verbatim: The smartest kid in my school had an IQ of 70 and he was currently laughing at my test. An F again. He held up his paper. A giant red A+. Then he pointed at mine. A giant red F. The entire class started laughing. I looked down at my paper, then at the glowing number above his head. 70 IQ. I looked at my reflection in the classroom window. 160 IQ. Yeah, something was seriously wrong here. But let me explain.
hook.device: In-medias-res cold open of the thumbnail scene + paradox statement ('smartest kid ... IQ of 70') in sentence one, then the visual payoff (red 70 IQ tag pops at 0:02, green 160 IQ in the window reflection at 0:28), then a 'But let me explain. It all started that morning…' rewind (0:32). The opening loop is closed at 3:18 when the story catches up to the cold open.
hook.visual: 0:00 wide classroom with caption chip 'THE SMARTEST KID IN SCHOOL' over Oliver; 0:02 close-up of Oliver with red '70 IQ' pill; inserts of the A+ and F papers held up; 0:28 reflection shot with green '160 IQ'; 0:30 wide two-shot showing both tags at once (red 70 vs green 160) = the thumbnail moment.

beats.summary: Flash-forward to the thumbnail scene: 70-IQ class star waves an A+, 160-IQ narrator gets an F, class laughs; both IQ tags revealed; 'something was seriously wrong here. But let me explain.'
That morning: sees mom's 112 IQ, rubs eyes, mirror shows 160. Googles it (bell-curve card: 'extremely high / genius territory'), feels vindicated, then remembers failing three tests this month (gag).
Home world-building: dad 118, the dog has no number and walks into a chair ('some things didn't need measuring').

Walk to school reading strangers' IQs with a comedic twist on each (businessman 125, construction worker 138, woman losing to a parking meter 146, guy pushing a PULL door 91). 'The world made sense. Or at least I thought it did.' (re-hook)
Best friend Jake asks his number (94); narrator lies 'above average'. Establishes lovable-dumb sidekick for comic relief.
Oliver: class president, perfect grades, top of every exam list - IQ 70. Narrator stares; Oliver mocks him about today's test he forgot. Jake: 'So this test should be easy.' (setup for irony)
'Three hours later' - story catches up to the cold open: F vs A+, 'How is this possible?' (central question restated at 3:37).
Library research: IQ is not knowledge, hours studied or homework done. Self-own: he rushed the test and drew a dinosaur in the margin. Reframe: Oliver isn't a genius, he's prepared.
A week of real studying (no phone/no games/no distractions), Jake helps; he solves hard problems fast but lacks basics ('spaceship without a screwdriver'); starts from the beginning.
Next test: Oliver A+, narrator an A - first earned A in years; Oliver doesn't laugh this time. 'That should have been the end. But then…' (re-hook).
Principal announces the National Student Challenge: city-wide, logic/maths/memory, full scholarship worth more than his parents earn in a year.
School needs a second contestant; narrator raises hand, class laughs, Oliver sneers 'Let's see what you've got.' Wins the qualifier by two points; Oliver isn't first for once and hates it.
Saturday, city auditorium full of glowing numbers (125, 140, 152, a 174-IQ girl). Jake (94) gives a thumbs up - comic warmth before the contest.
Round 1 maths: Oliver better. Round 2 memory: Oliver incredible. Round 3 logic: narrator finishes with 10 minutes left; scores put him 1st, Oliver 4th. Oliver looks scared, not angry (re-hook).

Backstage hallway: Oliver whispers 'If I lose, I'm finished'; shows dad's text 'Don't embarrass this family'; studies to 3 A.M.; 98% gets 'where did the other 2% go'. 'I wish I could be like you.' Narrator stops seeing the number: 70 isn't the most important number in the room.

Final round, same puzzle (2, 6, 12, 20, ?). Oliver sees his expressionless father in the front row, chokes, buzzes wrong (INCORRECT). Narrator has one answer left, sees Oliver's wet eyes - 'I couldn't solve his life for him' - and answers: CORRECT.
Auditorium erupts, Jake screams so loud security asks him to sit; Oliver stares at the floor; trophy handover.
Narrator takes the mic: failing doesn't mean worthless, being good at school doesn't make you better; credits Oliver as the reason he studied. Applause; Oliver confused at being thanked.
After the ceremony: Oliver apologises ('Extremely.'), asks how he got good at logic ('Trade secret'), they agree to study together; Oliver's first real laugh.
One month later, library: Oliver teaches history dates, narrator teaches logic, Jake asleep on a textbook; the numbers are still there but matter less.
'Intelligence can help you solve a problem, but it doesn't make you disciplined… kind… happy.' Both were wrong about what mattered.
Jake wakes: 'Wait, did we have homework?' - 'Some people really do need a little extra help.'
Direct question to viewers, also as on-screen text: if you could see everyone's IQ, would you want to know yours, and would you treat people the same way? (comment bait)

pacing.cut_detection: ffmpeg scene>0.25 on 160px proxy; includes paper/chip slam-ins and punch-ins, so 'visual changes' rather than pure camera cuts
pacing.notes: Fast and even: 20-34 visual changes per minute through the setup and competition, dropping to 14-16/min in the emotional backstage scene (7:46-9:24) and the closing moral, then speeding back up for the final round (30/min). Re-hook lines every ~45-90 s ('Or at least I thought it did', 'That should have been the end. But then…', 'he looked scared'). Narration is continuous, short declarative sentences (avg ~7 words), lots of one-word beats ('Still there.' 'Way.' 'Extremely.').

techniques_worth_copying: Number-above-head pill tag as the series' visual hook: one reusable component (green/red by threshold, pointer triangle, pop-in scale) that pays off the title in every scene and lets the viewer 'use the power' with the narrator.
Cold open on the thumbnail paradox, then 'But let me explain. It all started that morning…', and close the loop ~3 minutes in so the click promise is honoured early.
Rules-of-the-power gag run (mom, dad, dog with no number, strangers each with a twist) before the plot - cheap, quick, funny world-building at ~1 gag per 5 s.
Paradox premise that flips into a moral: the gimmick (IQ) is the lure, the payload is a relatable theme (effort vs. talent, pressure from parents) that drives comments.
Antagonist-to-ally arc with a mid-video sympathy reveal (dad's text on a phone insert) - the emotional turn sits at ~55-65% runtime.
Game-show climax visuals (rounds, scoreboards, countdown timer, INCORRECT/CORRECT full-frame cards) give long-form story a familiar escalating structure.
Dark navy line-art 'explainer cards' (bell curve, IQ ≠ KNOWLEDGE, spaceship/screwdriver metaphor, DAD vs 98% dilemma) to visualise abstract ideas in 2-4 s inserts.
Time/place caption chips ('THAT MORNING', 'THREE HOURS LATER', 'ONE WEEK LATER', 'THE BREAK · HALLWAY BACKSTAGE') make a 14-min single-narrator story easy to follow.
Hand-held paper inserts (tests with red grades, results sheets with a red circle, phone message) as the main 'evidence' shots - very cheap to make, very readable.
Comic sidekick (Jake, 94 IQ) as release valve after every tense beat, and as the final button joke before the CTA.
Ending CTA as on-screen two-part question about the viewer themselves ('would you want to know yours?') over the final tableau.
code_only_remake_needs: Stickman character rig in SVG/React: ball head (circle) with eye/eyebrow/mouth expression presets (neutral, smug side-eye, shocked O-mouth, sad, teary, determined squint, laughing), hair overlays (curly, slicked stripes, white), body = clothing shape per character + thin limbs with a few poses (sit, stand, walk cycle, arm raised, point, hold paper, kneel, thumbs-up). Mouth-flap on narration/dialogue.
IQ tag component: rounded pill with number + 'IQ', colour by threshold (green >=100, red <100), pointer triangle, spring pop-in, optional glow/fade-out; supports many tags at once over a crowd.

Flat vector background set (SVG): classroom (chalkboard, clock, posters, windows, desks), school hallway with lockers + banner, library shelves, bedroom (day/night), kitchen, city street with storefronts, auditorium stage with podiums/banners/spotlights/big screen, backstage corridor. Each with a blurred variant for close-ups (CSS/SVG gaussian blur on the background layer = fake depth of field).

Insert-shot templates: paper test with red ink grade + X/✓ marks + handwritten answers, results list with red circle animation, phone with message bubble, calendar, contestant list paper, money stacks, gloved hand holding object (slide-in from bottom).

Navy infographic card kit: thin white line-art icons (brain, book, rocket, screwdriver, stick figure), bell curve with marker, ≠ glyph, outlined uppercase chip labels, path draw-on animation (stroke-dashoffset), dotted grid map with nodes.

Game-show UI kit: round title screens, score lower-thirds, sequence-recall digit board, shape grid, countdown timer, full-frame INCORRECT (magenta, X) / CORRECT (green, ✓) cards, arcs with difference labels for number sequences.
Caption chip system for time/place cards and lower-thirds (uppercase, small, tracking), plus end-card typography (white + yellow uppercase, two lines).
Camera: Remotion transform-based push-ins, snap punch-ins to extreme close-up, lateral pans across wide backgrounds, cross-blur transitions; colour grading filter for desaturated flashbacks.

Audio: one first-person narrator VO (Kokoro/Piper) at ~145-150 wpm with per-character dialogue delivered by the narrator, continuous soft piano/orchestral bed with swells, a few SFX (buzzer, crowd cheer, paper slide, pop for tags).
Scale: ~325 visual changes over 14 min means the storyboard must be generated from the script (one shot per sentence on average) with reusable scene/pose presets rather than hand-placed shots.
